utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Good morning. May I ask the registrar to call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you. Good morning, Your Honours. This is Case Number IT-02-60-A, the Prosecutor versus Vidoje Blagojevic and Dragan Jokic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: I thank you. Can the -- Mr. Blagojevic and Mr. Jokic follow the proceedings in a language they understand? Is everything okay with the ...

utterances.speaker: THE APPELLANT BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE APPELLANT JOKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can, Your Honour. I understand you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Now, we resume our hearing, and I will briefly summarise how we proceed today. First, counsel for Jokic will have time to reply to the Prosecution's response for 20 minutes. Then counsel for the Prosecution will present its appeal for one hour, ten minutes. Later the response of -- will follow from Blagojevic and then for Jokic. And then we'll have the reply. At the end, both Mr. Blagojevic and Mr. Jokic, if they so wish, can make a personal statement for a maximum of ten minutes each. So now we will invite counsel for Jokic to present his reply to the Prosecution. You have the floor, Mr. Murphy.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning. Good morning, Your Honours, counsel. I will be very brief in replying to Ms. Issa's very able submissions on behalf of the Prosecution. It appeared, Your Honour, that there is no essential difference in principle between the Prosecution and the Defence as far as the legal issues are concerned that I addressed yesterday. I think we are in broad agreement as to the definition of aiding and abetting. I take it that the Prosecution still maintains, as they said in their brief, that there is no separate requirement of specifically directed. We maintain that the Trial Chamber was correct in holding that the acts of the accused must be specifically directed, and we believe, as we set out in our reply and indeed in our appellant brief, that the previous decisions of the Appeals Chamber amply support that position. And the Prosecution has really -- advanced no ground for the Appeals Chamber to differ from those previous decisions in this case. We also believe, Your Honour, that there is no essential difference in principle as regards the necessity for a prior agreement in cases where the acts are ex post facto. The Prosecution had suggested in its brief that perhaps there were other ways, other than a prior agreement, in which liability could be sustained; but the only practical suggestion that they made in that regard was what happens perhaps if the accused makes an offer of help. And in this context, we submit that there's really no difference between that situation and the situation where there is an agreement. And we remind the Trial Chamber in any event that there was no evidence in the record to support either an agreement or a prior offer of help by Mr. Jokic. I also understand, Your Honour, that the Prosecution does not differ from us on legal grounds with regard to our submissions about the burden of proof in relation to the fifth ground of appeal, certainly insofar as the rule is, of course, that the Prosecution bears the burden of proving the actus reus of the offence beyond all reasonable doubt. And so, I understood the Prosecution's submissions to be based essentially on factual grounds. And once again, as they did in their brief, the Prosecution sought to emphasise what they refer to as the overall murder operation. They painted a picture for Your Honours again of the horrific circumstances of Srebrenica from the time when the safe area, the protected area, was overrun through to the execution of the victims. And they do that in order to seek to persuade the Appeals Chamber that Mr. Jokic's involvement was in fact greater than the Trial Chamber found it to be. And so, Your Honour, we come back once again, as we must, to consider what the Trial Chamber actually found. And I respectfully remind the Appeals Chamber once again that in paragraph 770 of the judgement, the Trial Chamber found unequivocally that Mr. Jokic did not play a major role in this case. And despite the Prosecution's rhetoric, both in their brief and in Ms. Issa's submissions yesterday, that remains the starting point from which the Appeals Chamber has to begin to consider the issues. There was a murder operation, but Mr. Jokic was not convicted of a murder operation; he was convicting of aiding and abetting with respect to three particular sites. He was not convicted of being part of a joint criminal enterprise, whether that was based upon his role as duty officer or his role within the Engineering Company. And I remind the trial -- the Appeals Chamber, because this perhaps may be overlooked, was not referred to explicitly yesterday, of the Trial Chamber's findings that as duty officer, Mr. Jokic was not in a position to give orders. He had no authority to order other officers, whether it was Milosevic or Lazarevic or anyone else, to do anything. And the Trial Chamber explicitly found that he was not responsible for the wider joint criminal enterprise. And I have to keep coming back to what, with all respect, is the obvious because the Prosecution seeks to make this, in a way, the pillar of their submissions. And I remind the Appeals Chamber that the Prosecution has not sought to appeal against the Trial Chamber's finding that Mr. Jokic was not guilty of a joint criminal enterprise. Such a ground was initially contained in the notice of appeal, but it was explicitly abandoned and it does not form any part of the case that Your Honours are hearing today. Ms. Issa also submitted that the burials were, in her words, an essential component of the crimes. Now, Your Honours, the burial may have been a constituent part of the joint criminal enterprise. We don't know what was in the mind of those who were part of that joint criminal enterprise. We don't know to what extent the issue of burial played a part in the plans that were hatched at the Fontana Hotel and elsewhere before Mr. Jokic had any involvement. That's not part of the case against Mr. Jokic because burial is not, in fact, a legal component of the crimes which he was convicted. The Prosecution may argue that factually it was a component of the joint criminal enterprise, but I remind Your Honours again that that is not part of the conviction of Mr. Jokic. Ms. Issa drew Your Honours' attention to the issue of reburial and the observations of the Trial Chamber at paragraph 730 of the judgement, and she pointed out the Trial Chamber's finding that the reburials were the -- were not the subject of a prior agreement. And I think her intent was to argue that the issue of prior agreement was really more appropriate to the issue of reburial than it was to the initial burial of the bodies. Now, if Your Honours look at paragraph 730 of the judgement, you will see that that passage in fact refers to a finding with respect to Colonel Blagojevic, not to Jokic at all, and it is, in fact, indeed talking about the reburials. Nonetheless, we -- we submit, Your Honour, that the issue of prior agreement is a legal issue that applies over the whole spectrum of the case. It's not limited to the issue of reburial; it is limited -- it is indeed something that applies to any example of ex post facto assistance. And I remind the Appeals Chamber again that it does not appear to be a matter of dispute that a prior -- that certainly some form of prior agreement or arrangement or more evidence is required in the case of ex post facto assistance. The Prosecution also sought to persuade the Trial Chamber -- the Appeals Chamber that this was not a case of ex post facto assistance, and they offered to Your Honours a rather complicated chart, showing various activities that they ascribe to Mr. Jokic over a period of four days. The interesting thing about that chart, if you look at it in detail, is that, unlike the simpler one that we offered, it does not refer to the crucial issue of time, the times at which different events occurred. And if Your Honours go back to the paragraphs of the judgement that we referred to yesterday, and if it will be of assistance, I will be happy to provide a copy of our visual chart for the Appeals Chamber. I haven't printed it out, but I would be certainly glad to give one to the Legal Officer so that Your Honours will have it. If Your Honours will refer to the paragraphs of the judgement that are referred to there, you will see very clearly that in the case of the Pilica school and Kozluk, any acts of assistance which Mr. Jokic may have rendered were clearly ex post facto with respect to the commission of the offences. And I bear in mind the distinction that His Honour Judge Shahabuddeen made to me in a question yesterday between murder and extermination. But I say again, Your Honours, that as far as the legal definition of the crimes is concerned - and that's the crucial thing - the crimes were complete when Mr. Jokic, on the Prosecution's own case, rendered whatever acts of assistance he did. And, Your Honour, it comes in the end to this, that taking the case for the Prosecution at its highest and taking the findings of the Trial Chamber as they are, rather than as the Prosecution would wish them to be, the case against Mr. Jokic was essentially based upon an allegation that he was an accessory after the fact, a separate offence in both common law and civil law jurisdictions and one that, for whatever reason, is not included in Article 7(1) of the Statute of this Tribunal. And it follows from that, in our submission, that Mr. Jokic should be acquitted. Even if Your Honours are against me on the generality of that proposition, adopting the distinction suggested to me by Judge Shahabuddeen yesterday, I would submit that certainly in the case of the murder conviction, there can be no doubt that that conviction cannot stand. And I invite Your Honours to consider that as a separate issue. Your Honours, if there are any further questions from the Bench about any aspects of my submissions, I would be very happy, of course, to answer them now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Murphy. Judge Meron.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Murphy, for your very clear argument. You will recall that both today and yesterday you referred to the burials, to the question of burials. And yesterday you presented the question of burials as something which was necessary to avoid worse consequences, which I understood to be the public health, based on the public health rationale. Now, is this not actually a claim of necessity which we should regard as affirmative defence on your part and where the burden of proof would be on the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Your Honour, that would be a way to look at it if it were not a case of ex post facto assistance. In other words, I understand that the defence of necessity is more related to a case of perpetration where the accused says, Well, I did commit the offence, I did commit the crime, but there was a situation in which it was necessary to do so. And, as Your Honour rightly says, in that situation, of course, the Defence would have the burden of proving that affirmative defence. Your Honour, I present this case in a somewhat different way, and again, I respectfully remind the Appeals Chamber that the -- that I do this on a hypothetical basis to invite the Appeals Chamber's ruling as a matter of principle, not to suggest that this was actually a matter of Mr. Jokic's individual motivation. But assuming the facts to be as they were, the Prosecution had the burden of proof to show that what Mr. Jokic did amounted to an act of substantial assistance. It was an act that was still ex post facto, but I think the Appeals Chamber could regard it in the -- in this light, that if what Mr. Jokic did was not in fact an act of assistance but an act which anyone in his position had to do for other reasons, then it should not be regarded as a criminal act. The Prosecution has not proved the actus reus. Reus, of course, as Your Honour knows, meaning a guilty act. And in a way it also raises a question of principle. As a matter of policy, do Your Honours wish to make a ruling that will have the effect in future cases that a person -- let's assume a person with absolutely no association to the main crime at all, let's assume hypothetically a member of the public who happens to have access to some equipment had come along, having no responsibility for the murders whatsoever, and said, I will take responsibility for burying the bodies. Now, the Prosecution then could say, Well, that was an act which assisted the perpetrators, which is what they say in Mr. Jokic's case, which in a sense is true. And then the Prosecution would say, as they did yesterday, It doesn't matter what his motivation is, it doesn't matter that the act was lawful, per se, it was an act that assisted the perpetrators. And I would submit, Your Honours, that in that case, as a matter of principle, the Court should say, We do not wish to criminalise that act. There must be a line to be drawn somewhere because, if we don't draw it, the effect of our ruling will be that the already terrible consequences of such an act will be made even worse because that member of the public would be fearful of prosecution if he were to intervene to try to make the situation better. And I invite Your Honours to look at it also in that light.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Thank you. Judge Shahabuddeen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] I think you said that the Trial Chamber unequivocally found that Mr. Jokic did not play a major role in this case, and I believe you referred to paragraph 770. Now, is that the paragraph you intended to refer to?

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Your Honour is quite right. I misspoke. It's paragraph 836.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Your Honour is absolutely right. It was the sentencing paragraph in which the Trial Chamber made that observation. I'm very grateful to Your Honour for pointing that out. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Well, I believe if there are no other questions we can conclude the appeal of Mr. Jokic and move on to the appeal of the Prosecution. We'll give the floor to the Prosecution to present their appeal. You have the floor, Mr. Farrell.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Your Honours, the Prosecution appeal, as you're aware, consists in the appeal brief of -- and the notice of seven grounds of appeal. This morning the Prosecution will address five of those grounds in oral argument. It will not address in oral argument ground five -- I'm sorry, the -- it's subsection 5 of the appeal brief, it's the ground of appeal against Mr. Jokic as to his acquittal for the killings at Petkovci school and Petkovci dam. We maintain our submissions in our brief. I also will not be making any submissions this morning on the seventh section of the appeal brief, which relates to the application of Rule 92 bis. I've informed Mr. Murphy this morning that we won't be making any arguments with respect to the Petkovci school and dam ground against Mr. Jokic, but we'll simply rely on our brief. But that we will be making submissions as to sentence both to -- in relation to Mr. Blagojevic and in relation to Mr. Jokic. The three grounds that I will be making submissions on this morning for the Prosecution will be the first ground of appeal, which is the mass killings; the second ground of appeal, which is the intent to commit forcible transfer; and the third ground of appeal, the alleged errors with respect to Article 7(3) of the Statute. Then my co-counsel Mr. Costi will be making submissions at the end of the Prosecution's 70 minutes on sentence. If I may now proceed with respect to ground -- the first ground of appeal. And though the grounds of appeal in the brief start with the mass killings, which is chronologically after the forcible transfer, I intend to follow the structure in the brief, which is to start with the ground of appeal with respect to the mass killings. And the issue in that ground of appeal is whether or not the Trial Chamber erred in finding that Mr. Blagojevic did not have the requisite mens rea of knowledge for aiding and abetting the mass killings. As is evident from the Prosecution's brief, the position taken is that the events of Mr. Blagojevic's involvement over the period of the 11th to the 14th of July, 1995, point to one inescapable conclusion, that the appellant had knowledge about what was to happen to the Bosnian Muslim men when members of the Bratunac Brigade transported these men to detention facilities around Zvornik and where they were eventually killed. As you know, Colonel Blagojevic was the commander in the zone of responsibility where thousands of Bosnian men are captured and detained. He's found to have knowledge of involvement of the search, of the capture, of the detention, of the abuse, and of the killings, and that throughout the period, he received regular reports, apprised himself of them, and that the lines of communication were working properly. The Trial Chamber concluded, despite this, that they had a reasonable doubt as to his knowledge of the mass killings. Though it's evident that the Appeals Chamber, in relation to factual findings, should be hesitant to interfere with factual findings at the trial level, this court in the Kordic Appeals Chamber indicated that when it comes to a legal error with respect to the application of a factual mistake, that if the legal error has been established, this Court has an obligation then to review the trial record in totality and make a determination itself whether or not it would be reasonable to conclude that Mr. Blagojevic or whether or not on the record the accused or appellant had the requisite mens rea. The Prosecution has raised a ground of appeal in its -- sorry, an error of law in this ground of appeal. And if successful, it would require the Appeals Chamber, in our submission, to review the record, which would result in no deference to the findings by the Trial Chamber and the standard is not one of whether or not the Trial Chamber's findings were reasonable. That error, which I'll come back to at the end of my submissions, is that the Trial Chamber did not apply the correct standard for the mens rea of aiding and abetting. In this regard, though I won't take you to it, if you look at paragraph 727 of the Trial Chamber's judgement - and once again I won't take you to it - but also reference to 729, 742, 743, and 744. What you'll find, in the Prosecution's submission, is that the Trial Chamber is looking for actual knowledge on the part of Mr. Blagojevic. They're looking to see whether in fact he did know in the sense of actual knowledge. In the Prosecution's submission, this was an error. The standard is set out in the Blaskic Appeals Chamber judgement and, subsequently, in this Chamber's decision in the Simic case is that for the mens rea for aiding and abetting, in terms of the knowledge of the commission of the crime, is that the accused has to be aware that the crime - in this case the killing - was one of a number of crimes that would probably be committed. He doesn't have to know the specific crime; he has to turn his mind to the crime and be aware of its probability, accept those results, and on that basis assist. The Trial Chamber didn't apply this standard. Though specifically referring to Blaskic in paragraph 727, the Trial Chamber refers to Blaskic, the Appeals Chamber judgement, and makes references to paragraphs 45, 47, and 48 of the Blaskic Appeals Chamber decision. It makes no reference to paragraph 50 of the Blaskic Appeals Chamber decision, which specifically sets out the awareness of a probability standard in relation to the commission of a crime and the acceptance of that probability as a manner to conclude that the -- or that an accused would have the mental state for aiding and abetting. The Trial Chamber found all other elements were met. The only thing that was missing with respect to the murders was his mens rea. The second error that's raised and which I'll touch on briefly is simply an error of fact, and of course in that case, the Prosecution must prove that no reasonable trier of fact could have reached the conclusion, that is that even if there was no error with respect to the application of the correct mental standard, that on the facts as they are and on the evidence, no reasonable trier of fact could have concluded that Mr. Blagojevic did not have knowledge of the killings when the acts of his subordinates assisted. I'd like to deal with the error of fact first, strict error of fact. And the position is that the evidence conclusively points in only one direction and that's knowledge, actual knowledge. I ask that you please recall that this is one overall operation. There's not two separate operations here. There's no troops that are working alone or in isolation from each other. A number of units operated within the zone of responsibility of the Bratunac Brigade, commanders met at the Bratunac Brigade headquarters, tasks were given, and the attack, the forcible transfer of the women and children, searching the terrain, the guarding of prisoners, the transporting of men to Zvornik for their execution, they were all one orchestrated operation. In relation to this one operation, what was the Bratunac Brigade involved in? With the exception of the actual shooting during the executions, the Bratunac Brigade was involved in every aspect right through to the transfer and detention in Zvornik of those who were to be killed. What had the Trial Chamber found that Blagojevic knew? The Trial Chamber found that Blagojevic knew all aspects of the operation but one. Blagojevic was informed of the blocking of convoys. He was informed of the objective to eliminate the enclave. He commanded his troops during the attack on Srebrenica and was informed in advance of the operation and the units that were to be involved. He was apprised of the search operations as one of the brigade commanders participating in that operation. He was informed of the detention of the men captured in the search operation. He was aware of the killings in Bratunac. He was aware that the Bratunac Brigade were transporting the men to Zvornik. And he was informed that the women and children were taken in a different direction. He was informed of all of these activities because it was necessary that he be kept informed as the commander. Despite being informed of all these activities, the Trial Chamber found it was unreasonable to conclude that Blagojevic would be informed of why he was involved in the capture of men, why his men were transporting them to Zvornik, and what the purpose was. We submit that the evidence is overwhelming, that not only was he informed, but he would have to be informed. The Trial Chamber appears to have a doubt, at least in paragraph 742. One of the doubts they have or the basis of their doubt is that it was reasonable to conclude that he saw these actions as a further step in transporting the Bosnian Muslim population out of the Serb territory. Well, with respect, the men are actually not being transported out of the Bosnian -- out of the Serb-held territory; they're being transported further into the Serb-held territory up into Zvornik. The women and children are, but not the men. How the Trial Chamber came to this conclusion that it was reasonable for Blagojevic to assume this is unexplained. Blagojevic did not testify; that is his right, of course, but there's no evidence as to the basis of his action. Nor did anyone testify to any conversation with Blagojevic or knowledge they had of the reasons why Blagojevic was involved and what he understood the operation to be. Further, if the goal of transporting the men out of the Serb-held territory -- if the goal was to transport the men out of the Serb-held territory, why were the men not transported with the women to Potocari? Why did they have to bring in 70 -- 80 to 120 buses and detain them overnight in Bratunac? Let me take one of the findings by the Trial Chamber briefly to try and deal with the findings about the Kravica warehouse. Now, I've already submitted that based on the evidence and the findings of the overall operation, Mr. Blagojevic would have known and did know. Secondly, it's the Prosecution's position that he had knowledge of the killings at Kravica warehouse. The Trial Chamber found that he did not. But if he did have knowledge of the killings at Kravica warehouse, on July 13th, he would have known the purpose of the operation. Now, Kravica warehouse is in his zone of responsibility; it's not in Zvornik. Kravica warehouse is where a thousand men were killed. Kravica warehouse is 10 kilometres from his command post and is approximately 1 to 2 kilometres from the command post of his 4th Battalion. I'd just like to refer to one of the exhibits, which is a map. It's P16.1. And I've just asked that it be brought up on e-court. If you switch to the e-court button on your -- thank you. Obviously you've been able to find it. Okay. Thank you, Your Honour. Just to put in context the Kravica warehouse massacre. As you can see on the map, there is the town of Srebrenica, then from Srebrenica to Potocari is a total of 4 kilometres. From Potocari to Bratunac is around 3 kilometres. The town of Bratunac, a place where there's 80 to 120 buses overnight is 2 square kilometres, the size of the town. From Bratunac to Glogova, which is the burial site of the men from Kravica, is approximately 5 kilometres. The distance from the burial site to the massacre, that's Kravica on the map, is 5 kilometres as well. And the distance from Sandici, that's the meadow where the men were captured and where they were -- after capture, they were taken to Kravica for the massacre. From Sandici to Kravica is 2 kilometres. The Trial Chamber makes specific findings as a result of the order of the Drina Corps, this order coming from obviously the Drina Corps command, presumably Krstic, makes specific findings that as a result of an order from the Drina Corps, the commanders are to be informed of the events that take place in their zones of responsibility. And the Court finds that as a result of that order, Mr. Blagojevic would have known that there were a thousand men that were captured and detained in Sandici. The Court also finds that he would have known that they were not only captured but then were detained. Now, why they don't then make the conclusion that if he has to be informed of this and if they make a finding of fact that he is informed of their capture and detention, that he's not informed of what they did with them. Approximately 1.000 men are taken from Sandici to Kravica, either by buses or marching those thousand men to Kravica warehouse. They're placed in the warehouse, and the thousand men, over a period of time, are executed. The killings take four hours. There's shooting, grenades, machine-gun fire. Now, while this is going on, on the night of the 13th and then on the morning of the 14th - and if I could just step back - and then on the morning of the 14th, there's, as I understand, some final killings and then the burial operation starts for Kravica warehouse. The burial operation takes two days. While this is going on in the morning -- well, I'm not sure of the time, I apologise -- on the 14th, an order is issued by Colonel Blagojevic. If I could just -- it's up on screen and if I could just pull up the passage. The order issued on the 14th said: "From its positions, the 4th Infantry Battalion will control the area in front of it spreading from Lupoglava spreading to Ravni Buljim and reaching for it as far as Mratinsko Brdo and Sandici." Now, I've pulled up an exhibit from the trial which shows the area in more detail. As you can see in the middle-top of the exhibit, the line in red going from right to left is the road coming from Bratunac. And as you're aware, Kravica warehouse is 10 kilometres along that road from the Bratunac Brigade headquarters. To the left of Kravica, there's Sandici, and as I've indicated, it's somewhere between 1 to 2 -- it's approximately 2 kilometres from the meadow to Kravica warehouse. Now, on the map you'll see that the location Kajici, K-a-j-i-c-i, that's the forward command post of the 4th Battalion. Now, in the order for the 14th, the forward command post is to search the terrain for Bosnian Muslim men in front of it from Lupoglava, which you can see on the bottom right-hand side, to Ravni Buljim, to Mratinsko Brdo, all the way up to Sandici. The warehouse is in between the forward command post and Sandici, the ultimate place where the brigade is to cover in their search. And this is the main road upon which people are being brought and captured. It's not reasonable to assume that on the morning of the 14th, or at least during the day on the 14th, Blagojevic is issuing an order to his troops to search in the area for Bosnian Muslim men where there's been fighting between the 28th Mountain Brigade of the Bosnian Muslim men and the Serb forces and not inform them that when they hear shots, machine-gun fire, or any other disturbances from around Kravica not to worry, this is not fighting with the Bosnian Muslims. It's not reasonable to assume that during an operation of this magnitude within the centre of his zone, within 1 to 2 kilometres from his 4th Battalion command, that they wouldn't know what is happening to those 1.000 men. On top of that, the Trial Chamber found that Mr. Blagojevic travelled on the Bratunac main road between the 13th and the 14th; this is the road where the men are detained. They found that it took two days to complete the burial. They found that the burial involved civilian protection workers from Bratunac and two Bratunac Brigade members. They found that there were several meetings held in Bratunac between the civilian authorities, that's Deronjic, and Momir Nikolic of the Bratunac Brigade to carry out the burial operation. And a witness testified that by the morning of the 14th of July, the people in the town of Bratunac already knew of it. How was it that the one person who must know to carry out his functions is the one person that didn't know? The explanation by the Trial Chamber that Blagojevic must have thought they were going to be transported out of the territory makes no sense, in my respectful submission. They were never transported out of the territory. They were not transported to Bratunac to be detained. They were killed 10 kilometres down the road from his command post in an area that his troops are searching, when the Court finds that he is informed of their capture and detention. These detainees he's informed of their capture and detention because he's -- it's necessary and it's pursuant to superior command's orders. But that he just didn't know what happened to them after that. Based on all the evidence, it's the Prosecution's submission that he would have been aware of the fate of the Bosnian Muslim men. It's unreasonable to conclude, that despite being informed of all the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Sorry, Judge Meron.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: I believe that you have completed your argument on this question of knowledge of mass killings.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: I am just coming to the end of it, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: I will wait until then because I would like to ask a question.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour. The submissions I've made -- and I'm finished with the exhibit on the e-court. The submissions I've made relate to the error of fact, that it was unreasonable, based on the overall operation and based on the specific operation and the killing of a thousand men in his zone, to conclude that he wasn't aware. Lastly, even if this Chamber finds that it was not unreasonable for the Trial Chamber to conclude that he didn't have actual knowledge, I revert back to my earlier submission, which is that he -- if they applied the law correctly, aware of the probability that the mass killings was one of a number of crimes that would have been committed, he would have been aware of that probability in light of all the evidence. Those are my submissions in relation to the first ground of appeal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Perhaps Judge Meron, you may put your question now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: And I will have an additional question later. Judge Meron.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Mr. Farrell, you are asking us to reverse the Trial Chamber on findings of fact which were quite exhaustively discussed by the Trial Chamber. In paragraph 498, the Trial Chamber concludes, "There is some evidence to establish that Colonel Blagojevic learned about the mass executions at the Kravica warehouse sometime after it occurred." I draw your attention to the temporal element. And then in paragraph 743, the Trial Chamber tells us: "Finally, there is insufficient evidence to establish that Colonel Blagojevic knew that the buses being escorted from Bratunac to Zvornik by members of the Bratunac Brigade military police were taking the Bosnian Muslim men to temporary detention centres in order to execute them." So -- and this is a very important question. It appears that according to the Trial Chamber, "Blagojevic lacks the knowledge of mass killings. What does he know? He knows that at least until after his acts are completed is that forcible transfers, separation of men from women, and confinement of men under bad conditions are going on, and he possibly knows also that a number of men have been killed at the school." On that basis, I have some problem with the argument you are making.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. There's no doubt that this Court should be hesitant to interfere with factual findings. The Trial Chamber went through, to some extent, the factual findings but maintain the position, and I appreciate the obvious hesitancy of Your Honour to interfere with those findings. But in light of the overwhelming evidence, in my submission, that Blagojevic was involved in every aspect -- I'm sorry, the Bratunac Brigade was involved in every aspect. Blagojevic was informed of every aspect, and the one that it appears he didn't -- he wasn't informed of was the result of the operation that he was carrying out, which was the searching of the men. In light of the fact that he was informed of every other aspect and involved in every other aspect, it's unreasonable to assume that without direct evidence, it's clear that's the Court's concern, without direct evidence, you can't draw an inference from the facts. That's the Prosecution's submission in a nutshell, though I appreciate your concern, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Thank you. Judge Shahabuddeen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: One question, Mr. Farrell. Would it be correct to understand your submissions this way, that the women and children were being taken out of Serb-held territory, but that the men were being taken further into Serb-held territory?

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: They were taken to Zvornik, which is within the Serb-held territory; they were not taken out towards the Bosnian-held territory. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: And the men and the women?

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: I'm sorry, the women were taken towards the Bosnian-held territory, which was to the west, and the men were taken to the north within the Bosnian Serb-held territory to Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: One other point which has to do with the question posed by Judge Meron. It seems to me that the Trial Chamber was not denying absolutely that Mr. Blagojevic knew of the executions in Kravica warehouse. What it was saying was, and I quote it: "It remains," this is from paragraph 742, the last sentence. "It remains possible that Colonel Blagojevic did not learn of this mass execution until two, three days after it happened." Does that throw a different colour on your submissions?

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. The colour still remains quite clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: In black and white. That it's not what he found out afterwards, it's that he would have had to know and did know everything during. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge Shahabuddeen, and Mr. Farrell. Mr. Farrell, may I put to you another question to be clear, 100 per cent, about your position on the mens rea for aiding and abetting. Is that your position that the standard of mens rea to be applied for aiding and abetting should be consistent with other forms of liability under 7(1) of the Statute, in particular ordering, instigating, and planning, which require only awareness of a substantial likelihood that the crime will be committed. And the second question: In your appeal brief, you submit that at a certain point, once you referred to the probability standard, and on another paragraph - I think it's paragraph 62 - you speak of awareness of substantial likelihood that the crime will be committed and knowledge or awareness of substantial likelihood that the acts of the accused will assist. Are you having a double substantial likelihood standard is what you are maintaining, or when we come to the assistance de facto that the acts will assist is just knowledge. Which is your position exactly?

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. That's not only an astute question, it's a fair one in light of that paragraph which left it open. So to answer your question, the first part of your question, the Prosecution maintains that for a matter of consistency and also because of the finding in Blaskic, that once you find the cognitive element of awareness of the substantial likelihood of that level, then the volitional element is to be regarded as having been met and that the standard should be the same. So it's an awareness of the substantial likelihood. With respect to the second aspect, there's two components to -- my understanding, there's two components to the mens rea. There's the awareness or knowledge of the crime, going to the crime, and there's awareness or knowledge that your acts assist. And the finding in Blaskic goes to the awareness of the probability in relation to the knowledge of the crime. It doesn't deal with the second aspect, which, as you are fully aware, Mr. President, from our brief, it doesn't deal with the second aspect in our submission as set out in our brief is that if the standard is accepted as awareness of a probability and the degree of risk is substantial likelihood, that should go to the component parts of the mens rea for aiding and abetting. So it should be awareness of a substantial likelihood of the crime and awareness of the substantial likelihood that your acts are assisting. And once you accept that, you then have the mens rea -- accept and act upon it in the dolus eventualis sense.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Judge Meron.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Mr. Farrell, if I may return for a moment to the question asked of you by my learned colleague Judge Shahabuddeen, who drew your attention to the last sentence of paragraph 742.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: "It remains possible that Blagojevic did not learn of this mass execution until two, three days after it had happened." This I would read together with the first sentence of -- in fact, the only sentence of paragraph 743, reading finally: "There is insufficient evidence to establish that he knew," et cetera, et cetera. Now, these senses or statements read to me as suggesting that prior knowledge by Blagojevic was not established beyond reasonable doubt, and do you agree that this should be read like that?

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I would -- I would agree with that, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: Mr. President, did I answer your questions?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Yes, I believe you answered my question clearly. I know your position now. Thank you for assisting.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: You may go on on your submissions, Mr. Farrell.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: Thank you. The two other grounds I wanted to touch on before handing the floor over to Mr. Costi -- excuse me for just one minute.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: The -- I apologise for the interruption. The second ground of appeal relates to the intent to commit forcible transfer. And once again, there's only a single issue in this ground of appeal, and that issue is whether or not he - that being the appellant, Mr. Blagojevic, the respondent to the Prosecution's appeal, I'm sorry - whether or not he had the intent to forcibly transfer and whether or not he shared the intent. Once again, this is a pure error of fact, and therefore the same concerns were -- deference the Court may have with respect to the findings would obviously apply. But in the Prosecution's submission, once again, there is really only one inference to the drawn by Colonel Blagojevic's actions, and that is that, as found by the Trial Chamber, Colonel Blagojevic knew of the objective, which was the elimination of the enclave; that this would necessarily entail removing the Bosnian Muslim population; and he implemented that operation. He didn't simply assist someone else's crime; he carried out the acts of the crime himself. He implemented the plan, which had as its objective the elimination of the enclave. As found by the Trial Chamber, he participated in the crime. He was not assisting it. In a situation where there's an overall operation of this magnitude, those who engage in it with knowledge and fulfil the purpose and take acts to fulfil the purpose, especially one that, as I'll indicate, arose from the acts for the two months prior and included acts right to the end of the forcible transfer, the only inference is that he intended the forcible transfer. He did all these acts to implement the forcible transfer but didn't intend for that to be the case. He ordered the shelling of Srebrenica before the events, but he didn't intend for it to cause the Bosnian Muslims to leave. He assisted in the blocking of the convoys that were going into the enclave, but he didn't intend for there to be the consequences that the Muslims would leave. His troops shelled and shot at the Bosnian Muslims as they fled from Potocari -- from Srebrenica to Potocari. The witness testified that he did that and he had the authority to do that under an order he received from Blagojevic on the 5th, but despite having done that, he didn't intend that it would force them to leave Srebrenica. In my respectful submission, the Trial Chamber engaged in an exercise of finding knowledge and not linking his acts with his mens rea. In light of the time-period, I'd just like to take you to a few passages in the judgement. If I could just ask you to turn to page 177, please, Your Honours, if you have the judgement in front of you; if not, I'll refer to it. This section is the first section that the Trial Chamber makes factual findings with respect to the mens rea. This section includes the factual findings from which they draw their conclusion with respect to the joint criminal enterprise. Now, without overstating the significance of this, I'd ask you simply to look at what the title is. The title of the section is not "factual findings as to his intent," the title of the section is not "factual findings as to the mens rea of Blagojevic." What they're looking for, their starting point is his knowledge of the actions of the Bratunac Brigade. If you then -- in light of the time, I'll just go through a few. If I can ask you to turn over to paragraph 476. It says: "The Trial Chamber furthermore finds that there is sufficient evidence to establish beyond a reasonable doubt that Colonel Blagojevic had knowledge that elements of the Bratunac Brigade, including the 2nd and 3rd Battalion, were involved in sniping and shelling of Srebrenica in the months before the enclave was attacked as well as in the attack on the DutchBat Observation Post Echo in early June. Under the operating practices in place within the Bratunac Brigade, Colonel Blagojevic would have met regularly with his subordinate commanders of the four battalions and would have received regular reports about their activities." With respect, he's not a passive recipient as a bystander receiving reports from his troops after it happens. The sniping and shelling that took place in Srebrenica, the Trial Chamber found, was a policy which he accepted and continued after he became the commander in May 1995. The attack on the Dutch Battalion in June 1995 was an attack by the Bratunac Brigade on UN peacekeepers. It was a coordinated attack and there's exhibits on the record which indicate that after the attack, the next day, Blagojevic is sending replacement troops up to the place where the operation -- where the observation post is, and in his final analysis of combat readiness report, he is reporting on the actions of the troops and taking over the DutchBat observation post. The Trial Chamber, in my respectful submission, deals with it as if he finds out after the fact. Paragraph 477, "The Trial Chamber finds that Colonel Blagojevic knew of the Bratunac Brigade's participation in the attack on the enclave." Well, with respect, this is inexplicable. He didn't know of the attack on the enclave, he wasn't informed after the fact that his troops happened to be involved in it. Colonel Blagojevic received instructions and issued orders on July 2nd to his subordinates and on July 5th to his subordinates at the Bratunac Brigade headquarters. Those are the findings. He didn't find out after the fact, as some passive recipient, who happens to realise that his resources are being used by someone else. And then as it goes forward in paragraph 477, it then says: "He knew that it had the effect of causing those civilians and DutchBat to take the decision to leave Srebrenica town and to go to Potocari and again while the civilians were fleeing from Srebrenica to Potocari." He finds in the next sentence that they were fired on on June 11th, and he was aware of that. These were his troops; they were carrying out the operation. The operation was to eliminate the enclave. The person who testified said that he was issued an order on the 5th of July which would authorise his shelling. Now, in his examination, that witness, Mr. Gavric, tried to downplay the objective of shelling but admitted that he shelled them and shelled, first of all, at them and then changed his direction and shelled around them. Once again, this isn't Mr. Blagojevic unaware, sitting in Belgrade being informed after the fact that there's troops on the ground and therefore he subsequently had knowledge. If you go through the judgement in subsequent paragraphs relating to his mens rea component, the Trial Chamber specifically approaches it on the basis of its looking for his knowledge. Now, to the fair to the Trial Chamber, in relation to whether or not he planned, ordered, or instigated, they found that those modes of liability were not applicable at the 98 bis stage. So it may have been looking at the issue from that perspective, but that doesn't apply to JCE. He can contribute in many mays, including ordering his troops to do acts, which may be even not illegal but which contribute to the JCE. The fact that the starting point is knowledge, the fact that the starting point is knowledge, indicates that the Trial Chamber didn't look at his acts for the purpose of determining his mental state; they determined first that he had knowledge and looked at the acts to see what he was informed about is as if he somehow received that information as a passive recipient after the fact. Let my submission be, when you go through both the facts and understand the approach taken by the Trial Chamber, this Court would conclude that no reasonable trier of fact could conclude on the acts of his implementation of Krivaja 95, those acts of participation, those acts of implementation that he somehow simply had knowledge of the effect of it, that he didn't intend it to happen, and that he didn't operate together with the other members of the JCE and shared the intent. I'll now move to the third ground.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: I defer to Judge Shahabuddeen.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Is there anything in the trial judgement which alludes to any dissociation of Mr. Blagojevic from the executions?

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: From him personally or individually?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: Not to my knowledge, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Oh.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: Thank you. Excuse me, Your Honour. I just wanted to check on how much time the Prosecution has left. I didn't make a note, I apologise, as to when we started.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: I believe you started at 8.27 -- 28, okay, if my recollection is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. That's quite precise, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: You can go to 9.38.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: Thank you. In relation to the third ground of appeal that the Prosecution presents in its appeal brief, the third ground of appeal relates to the application of Article 7(3) in relation to the acts of the Bratunac Brigade. Now, you recall that Mr. Blagojevic was not found guilty under 7(1) for aiding and abetting the murder operation, for aiding and abetting the murders and the extermination, as you're aware. And therefore, that issue fell to be decided under 7(3); that would be the issue that the Court would have to address to determine whether or not he was aware of the acts of his subordinates in relation to that operation and failed to prevent or punish. That's the focus of the ground of appeal because it's, in light of the other findings under 7(1), it's not necessary to determine whether or not he also subsequently knew of them under 7(3) because he obviously did; he was found guilty under aiding and abetting. The Trial Chamber found that members of the brigade did provide assistance and it found that Blagojevic became aware of the crimes committed by Momir Nikolic at some point in time after the fact. It doesn't indicate when. And it says that the -- he was aware of the crimes committed by Momir Nikolic, including persecutions. Now, persecutions is a legal characterisation, not the specific acts that he would have known. But in light of the fact that Count 5, persecutions, includes the acts of murder, it's - at least in the Prosecution's submission - apparent that what it was saying that all the underlying acts of persecution, including murder, were known to Mr. Blagojevic at some point in time. The Trial Chamber then finds, for reasons I'll go to, that it's -- it would be unreasonable to include that he had 7(3) liability. There's four issues that are raised in this ground. The first one relates to whether or not 7(3) liability is limited to only those cases where your subordinates commit, commit in the physical sense of perpetration. And I won't make any submissions on it. Your Honours are fully aware of it, and since the briefs have been filed, the decision by the Oric Trial Chamber has come out rejecting that proposition, as it has been rejected by the same Chamber in the Boskovski case and I'm aware that there's an interlocutory appeal before this Chamber on that issue already, so you're fully briefed of it. The second issue is that the Trial Chamber seems to indicate that it was unable to conclude that Blagojevic would know the exact identity of the perpetrators, and therefore he couldn't be found guilty under 7(3). Once again, in light of the Krstic Appeals Chamber judgement and the Delalic Appeals Chamber judgement, specifically that you only have to be put on notice of alarming information that your subordinates are committing crimes, submits that it's incorrect to determine -- or to conclude that unless you know the exact identity, you therefore do not have to inquire further. There are two other errors that just require a few minutes of submissions, in my opinion, and that's in relation to the determination of superior/subordinate relationship between Momir Nikolic and Mr. Blagojevic. If I could ask Your Honours to turn to paragraph 795. Paragraph 795 is the paragraph dealing with the liability of Colonel Blagojevic for the acts of Momir Nikolic. It begins with a finding that Momir Nikolic was a subordinate of Colonel Blagojevic. It proceeds to indicate that Momir Nikolic committed crimes, at least persecutions. It finds that the Trial Chamber at some point in time -- sorry, the Trial Chamber finds that at some point in time Colonel Blagojevic had knowledge of this, so therefore, he was put on knowledge of the crimes themselves. And then concludes that considering that during the period between July and November 1995, that senior members of the Bosnian Serb army were in the Srebrenica area issuing orders and instructions, and taking into consideration the Trial Chamber's findings in relation to the functional chain of command for the security organ, that's Momir Nikolic, not the military police, but the security organ. The Trial Chamber is unable to conclude that he had effective control. It then, three lines from the bottom, beginning with the words "moreover," states: "Moreover, while recognising that Colonel Blagojevic failed to take any measure to prevent or punish the crimes of Momir Nikolic, the Trial Chamber is convinced that a commander is not obliged to perform the impossible." No problem with that from the Prosecution, that proposition, but it's what continues that I take issue with: "And that reporting the matter to competent authorities may not have been in the circumstances at that time a reasonable measure that would have led to the punishment of Momir Nikolic." As you're aware, the Trial Chamber had earlier found that Momir Nikolic was within Blagojevic's chain of command and that the functional chain of command did not disturb that responsibility. It did recognise, though, that Momir Nikolic was receiving orders, that's correct, from members of the Bosnian Serb forces while on the ground, and that those orders were orders that he was given specifically while on the ground directed from the Bosnian Serb forces. It doesn't appear to be negating the previous findings about the functional chain of command, that it didn't affect the command and control, but that specifically for Nikolic in this case, it wouldn't have resulted in any result. The point that I simply wanted to make was if the Trial Chamber's finding is that the acts that are within your material ability have to be ultimately successful, that would not be a position that the Court should accept. The material ability would include the ability to initiate measures, those within your capacity or within your realm as a commander, and would include steps that don't reach the final result. The Trial Chamber's analysis of the act of reporting Momir Nikolic to the military justice authority comes to a halt because of the finding it may not lead to punishment. But if it appears that the ultimate result will be that the subordinate will not be prevented or punished, the question remains: Does that mean that a superior whose material ability includes reporting to superiors or reporting to military courts or initiating an investigation should be absolved of the responsibility of doing so? In the Prosecution's submission, the answer must be no. First, even if the steps which the commander is able to take may not result in the ultimate prevention of the crime, it could have other effects such as postponement of the crime. Second, a commander does not need to know whether it is certain that the crimes will be prevented or punished, and it can't be left if this is the inference to the subjective consideration of a commander to determine whether or not his acts will be beneficial to the prevention or punishment of the crime. Thirdly, the result seems illogical when you think of superior orders. Superior orders are not a defence. So a commander who accepts an illegal order and implements it can't raise superior orders as a defence. But a commander whose troops accept an illegal order and he finds out about it, if the order came from his superior, essentially he does have the defence of illegal orders, i.e., those illegal orders were given to my subordinates and even if I took action it wouldn't result in punishment. If you accept that analysis, Article 7(4) of the Statute, which is the defence of superior orders is not a defence, would only apply to ordering but would not apply to 7(3) liability. Take, for example, the recent case of Galic, and this is a purely hypothetical scenario. As you know, the evidence in that case and the findings arose from the acts over a period of time. There was some issue as to whether or not, in this hypothetical scenario, whether or not Galic himself ordered or whether he's liable under 7(3). If the campaign of persecutions of Sarajevo was a result of orders from the civilian or military superior, which clearly intended this to be the result, Galic would not be found guilty because any acts he did with his subordinates to prevent the shelling of Sarajevo would be useless. Simply conclude that the approach by the Trial Chamber was an error and that the Court should be cognizant of the fact that the material ability to prevent or punish does not look to the end result but looks to what's in their capacity to do and what means would be reasonable in the circumstances. In light of the time, if you have any questions, I'll be happy to assist; if not, I would like to allow Mr. Costi to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Yes, I see Judge Meron.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: If I may ask you for a -- to clarify for me, I must have missed something in the reply that you gave to the question asked of my distinguished colleague Judge Shahabuddeen. The question as you remember was whether there was anything in the judgement which would dissociate Blagojevic from mass execution. And your answer was, if I remember correctly, no, there isn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: Not that I'm aware of, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Right. Let me understand, mass executions means the same as mass killings?

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Now, didn't we already learn that the trial judgement in fact said that Blagojevic had no knowledge of that?

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: So isn't -- right. And I suppose there is nothing in the judgement which associates Blagojevic to the executions?

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: Well, besides his acts of assistance through his troops, but my understanding of Judge Shahabuddeen's question - I apologise for interrupting you - was whether or not there is any evidence on the record that he, as you're aware, dissociated himself. In other words, whether he took steps which would clearly indicate to the contrary, and there isn't any. With respect to your question, yes, it's true they didn't find knowledge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you very much. This is very helpful. President, I would like to ask one legal question. Do I have time to do that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Yes, proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you so much. I know that you did not raise this in your appeal, but the Defence raised it and the Defence yesterday made it very clear that they do maintain all the grounds of appeal raised in their briefs. And I would be extremely grateful if you could help enlighten us on a legal point which pertains to complicity of Blagojevic in genocide. Now, you will recall that the trial judgement concluded that for complicity in genocide to occur, the accused must have knowledge that his acts assisted in the commission of the specific crime by the principal offender and that the accused knew that the crime was committed with specific intent. The Trial Chamber then concluded that Blagojevic's knowledge of the goal of forcible transfer, along with his knowledge that the men were separated from the rest and detained under inhumane conditions, was enough to show knowledge that the crime of genocide occurred. Now, is this not an unduly broad view of genocide. Could you explain to me the basis for concluding that forcible transfers constitute genocide in this case. Aren't we watering down here -- hasn't the Trial Chamber watered down the concept of genocide if we deem forcible transfer of a population to be enough to constitute genocide? And let me tell you, I'm well aware of the judgement in the Krstic case, but there our decision was different from that.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I'll try to assist, though if I don't or if this issue is a matter that is of grave concern to the Court, I'd ask that we be given the opportunity to -- brief -- if of course it would assist Your Honour simply because it wasn't raised and it wasn't briefed. So I think my response is going to be more impressionistic than legal. The approach that -- first of all, let me set out the approach that I think is the appropriate approach to determine whether or not an accused would have mens rea in these circumstances. The issue isn't whether or not forcible transfer in and of itself constitutes or results in genocide. The issue is whether or not, based on the evidence, including the forcible transfer, one could infer the intent and that the focus should not be on whether certain acts do or don't constitute genocide and whether the forcible transfer of the population, as you've requested, is enough to constitute genocide. I think the starting point has to be whether or not there was an underlying act, which in this case there was, and whether or not there is sufficient basis to determine that the Court's finding from -- of the inference of the genocidal intent was reasonable. Now, in that case, in that respect, the focus isn't on whether or not reliance on forcible transfer would result in an unduly broad definition of genocide because it's not the completion of the act that we're concerned about with genocide, it's not what acts were taking place. We only need to look at the underlying acts. And so I would submit that the approach that should be taken in the way that I read the judgement was, despite those particular passages, the Chamber did find that there was a genocide on the basis of all the acts. And found that as a result of what Mr. Blagojevic knew at the time, even without the mass executions, he was aware of the genocidal intent of others. Now, whether that finding that he was aware of the genocidal intent of others or not is reasonable is an issue that may go to the ground of appeal raised by my learned friend, that in light of his lack of knowledge about the mass killings. But that's the assessment, and though the Trial Chamber does at one point in time engage in a discussion about the definition of what destruction means - and I do accept Your Honour's comments that they do talk about destruction in a manner which includes forcible transfer as the -- included in the act of the genocide itself - but what they then do is they then go back to the issue of whether or not on the basis of all the evidence on the record you can infer intent without the mass killings and that a genocide did happen. So they didn't venture into dangerous waters at the end of the day and they did apply it correctly, that being that, in light of all the evidence that was on the record as to his knowledge, he knew of the perpetrators' intent for the crime of complicity. Sorry, if that's not more helpful, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Farrell.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: I apologise for the shortness of time I've left Mr. Costi.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President. I'll just ask Mr. Costi to address you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour. May I ask you how many minutes I still have, like two, three, probably? No more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Well, your time will elapse in two minutes, but I think it's fair to give you five minutes more.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: I appreciate that. I will now address the Prosecution appeal on sentence. The Prosecution would first like to say that it maintains all the arguments addressed in the appeal brief in relation to sentencing; however, also in light of the recent appeal judgement in committing Galic, I wish not to reiterate only one aspect of the Prosecution's sentencing appeal. 18 years' imprisonment for Blagojevic and nine years' imprisonment for Jokic are manifestly inadequate sentences in light of the scale and gravity of the crimes and in comparison to the sentence imposed by this Tribunal. The Trial Chamber correctly stated at paragraph 818 that the gravity of the offence is the primary factor to be considered in determining the sentence. This was also recently confirmed by the Appeals Chamber in the Galic case at paragraph 442. The question on appeal as formulated in the Galic appeals judgement is whether the Trial Chamber gives sufficient attention to this factor in sentencing; if it did not, the sentence may be manifestly inadequate. And in a quote: "It is the Appeals Chamber's prerogative to substitute a new sentence when the one given by the Trial Chamber cannot be reconciliated with principle [indiscernible] sentencing." This is exactly the case for Blagojevic and Jokic. Colonel Blagojevic, he was found responsible for complicity in genocide, aiding and abetting murder, persecution, and inhumane acts. As commander of the Bratunac Brigade, he substantially contributed to the destruction of the Bosnian Muslim community in Srebrenica. He permitted his subordinates to be used for this purpose by those active with genocidal intent --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Please slow down for the interpretation. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: I'm sorry. And he knew that. He substantially contributed to the persecution and forcible transfer of 25.000 Bosnian Muslims through their capture, their detention, their physical and mental suffering. Blagojevic substantially contributed to the cruel and inhumane treatment of thousands, the separation, the fear and the terror on Muslim civilians, the transport of women and children, and the murder of more than 50 men. Blagojevic's sentence to 18 years does not reflect the scale of the crimes he was convicted for. Major Jokic, he was found guilty for aiding and abetting, extermination, murder, and persecution. He contributed as duty officer and chief of engineering through sending and monitoring the deployment of the Zvornik Brigade resources and equipment to the mass execution sites. This ensured the successful completion of the murder operation. He substantially contributed to the extermination of more than 3.000 Bosnian Muslims. Jokic's sentence to nine years is manifestly inadequate in light of the gravity of the crimes. Neither of the accused, as the Defence might try to argue, was the main architect of the crimes that occurred in Srebrenica, whether the mere fact that someone else played a more significant role in the extermination of 7.000 Bosnian Muslims and the destruction of an entire community does not undermine the gravity of the crime of which the accused are responsible. Comparing cases in sentencing is not always meaningful because differences between cases may make comparison very difficult. However, the Prosecution would mention two cases today: Momir Nikolic and Dragan Obrenovic. They were convicted for persecution in respect of the overall campaign in Srebrenica and sentenced to 20 and 17 years' of imprisonment respectively. They both pleaded guilty. They both showed remorse, and they both substantially cooperated with the Prosecution. Nikolic and Obrenovic helped the Tribunal to save time and resources. Nikolic and Obrenovic contributed to finding the truth and ultimately to achieve one of the goals of this Tribunal: Reconciliation. On the contrary, in the case of Blagojevic and Jokic, there are not such exceptional mitigating circumstances that might justify the relatively low sentence. The comparison of these cases, in the absence of significant mitigating factors in this case, demonstrate that the sentences imposed are manifestly inadequate. In this context, the point is not whether the Trial Chamber failed to compare this case with similar previous cases; the point is that by comparing these cases, it appears that the Trial Chamber failed to impose an adequate sentence. While the Trial Chamber has a wide discretion in sentencing process, this discretion is not unlimited. The Trial Chamber did not give sufficient attention to the magnitude and the gravity of the crimes. The Trial Chamber erred in finding that the sentence imposed adequately would reflect the gravity of the crime. For this reason, even if the Appeals Chamber were to conclude that all the other arguments raised by the Prosecution in the brief should be dismissed in relation to sentencing, should be dismissed, and even if it were to confirm all the findings that the Trial Chamber made in relation to sentencing, still the sentence handed down by the Trial Chamber should be regarded as manifestly inadequate. Jokic's alone shows that. He participated in the extermination of more than 3.000 people on a discriminatory basis; nine years' of imprisonment is manifestly inadequate. The Prosecution for these reasons respectfully requests this Chamber to increase Blagojevic's and Jokic's sentences to accord with the principle of sentencing of this Tribunal. And this ends my submission. I thank you for the five minutes I had in addition.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Costi. Judge Shahabuddeen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Counsel, I'm at page 299 of the trial judgement, which speaks at the top of aggravating circumstances. Is there anywhere in the trial judgement that reference is made to Srebrenica's status as a United Nations protected area? Has that factor any relevance at all to the concept of aggravating circumstances as employed in this case?

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Your Honours, I do -- I'm not aware whether the Trial Chamber did consider as an aggravating this element. The point is understanding the status of a safe area or protected area of Srebrenica. It is related to the commission of the crime for which he was convicted. If this is what the Appeals Chamber would consider or the Trial Chamber found, in that case, it might be considered as an aggravating factor and is not in the trial judgement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: I thank you. Well, there are no other questions. And looking at the clock, I believe that it's probably preferable to have the break now and to reconvene at 10.15 sharp to listen to the response of Mr. Blagojevic and then of Mr. Jokic. So the hearing is adjourned now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: We resume now the hearing, and as scheduled, I give the floor to counsel for Mr. Blagojevic for the response to the Prosecution's appeal. You have the floor, Mr. Domazet.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. Although, to an extent, it is difficult to speak about all this from the position of the Defence, which, as I said yesterday, believes justifiably that the accused did not have a fair trial and that the Defence now must evaluate and refer to evidence presented during the trial without any participation by the accused. When talking about ground 1 of the Prosecution's appeal regarding the mass killings and knowledge of mass killings, I would first like to say something about the area of responsibility. Unfortunately, Mr. Blagojevic, as the accused, did not have a military expert who would be able to explain that in detail, but it is evident that the Prosecution views the area of responsibility as the area in the entire sector, including Srebrenica, Bratunac, the entire geographic area, in the belief that the headquarters of the brigade is in Bratunac. This is erroneous because at the time of the operations of -- Operation Krivaja 95, each unit that participated, and it is well-known that there were many other units as well, thus that the Bratunac Brigade was just one of the military units. There were also police units there and special units, as you know, there that participated in this operation. The true area of responsibility is regulated by regulations, regulations referred to by the Prosecution as well and which were in force at the time and which were inherited from the JNA, and that is that during combat actions, the area of responsibility is the area in which the unit is assigned or is acting there. So the task of the Bratunac Brigade there was clear. The position of the company of the Bratunac Brigade, where they should be, as stated previously and is not disputed, the forward command post was at Pribicevac. It's a mountain which is located above Srebrenica, and these companies of the Bratunac Brigade each had their own positions in relation to Srebrenica where they were. Precisely, that area was assigned to the Bratunac Brigade, and that was their zone of responsibility in these actions. The Prosecution is trying to prove that the village of Kravica was in the area of operations of this brigade. Had this been so, at least one soldier or any unit would have been found there during the combat actions and during Krivaja 95 operation, and this is not the case. As far as I recall, the police unit was in Kravica, just as other units were in other locations. And they were all acting in accordance with orders by superior commands, according to which Blagojevic himself, as the commander of the Bratunac Brigade, also acted. So neither Kravica or any other places that are mentioned, Glogova, and so on, were not in the area of responsibility of the Bratunac Brigade. The town itself of Bratunac was not part of it. It was the seat of the Drina Corps and it was the seat of the forward headquarters or staff of the Army of Republika Srpska. But the actual, real zone of responsibility was where the actual Bratunac Brigade had its companies and its actions. This was not in Bratunac, other than the headquarters that existed there before the combat actions. There were no members of the brigade or soldiers of the brigade in Bratunac itself; they were at their assigned positions in the zone of responsibility. So this is the area of responsibility. Maybe during the trial, this was not clarified, and I think that as a consequence, we have the fact that the accused did not have a military expert who would be able to explain such matters. However, we are finding our conclusions on regulations which can be interpreted in this specific way. If the zone of responsibility, that term, was interpreted in a different way, then we would perhaps have a different angle. The assertion that he knew about the detentions, which is quite general and broad, if we are considering the capture of members carried out by the army, I must repeat what I already stated yesterday, and that is, when we're talking about the Bratunac Brigade and its assignments and the positions where it was, they did not encounter a single soldier of the 28th Division of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, had no actions in relation to them, and didn't have a single capture. So the Bratunac Brigade did not have a single captured soldier and absolutely no civilians that were captured either. When we're talking about the possibility of his knowledge, I believe that my learned friend from the Prosecution very frequently talked about the possibility of being aware of the probability, should have known, would have known. In my view, these are assumptions mostly because of his post as the commander of the brigade at the time. I would just like to recall not only the circumstances, such as the forward command post being quite far from Bratunac and from the positions of all of these other units.
