A little bit later I'm also going to refer to the same exhibit referred to by the Prosecution, and then I would like us then to look at the map that was already shown so that the Appeals Chamber could actually see where Pribicevac is, where this forward command post is, and how far it is from the area where the pull-out was underway of both members of the 28th Division and the civilians, where the column was intercepted, which is something that was discussed during the trial before the Trial Chamber. My learned friend mentioned as an argument that no reasonable trier of fact could establish that the accused did not have the opportunity to know about the killings, and even that the meetings were held in the Bratunac Brigade headquarters, if I understood correctly what was said. So I need to repeat this. The Bratunac Brigade headquarters was not the location of a single meeting. General Mladic, who did come several times to Bratunac, and this is well-known, held meetings with different officers, with representatives of DutchBat, and held these meetings with many security officers of the Zvornik Brigade, the Drina Corps, but he never held any meetings with Colonel Blagojevic, whether because he felt that this was not necessary in view of the assignments of the Bratunac Brigade in the operation or because he felt that Blagojevic was at his command post in Pribicevac - this is a separate question. But no meeting was actually physically held in the premises of the Bratunac Brigade headquarters. Of course, I said yesterday that the only meeting with some of the officers was on the 11th of July in the evening after 2200 hours when Blagojevic came from Pribicevac and encountered at his command post in his room General Krstic with a group of his officers. There they talked, and that is all that he was able to see of superior officers or anybody from the superior command until he left for Zepa with the brigade, because that was his next assignment. And straight from the positions where his brigade was, he left to assume another assignment in Zepa. When you look at the map - perhaps now is a good time to look at the map. I think this is Exhibit P16.1. Can we please look at this exhibit on the monitors. When you look at the place where Pribicevac is --

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: Excuse me, I'm sorry for interrupting. I'm just going to see if we can assist by getting the map up. It's not on the screen, Mr. Domazet, as I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: It's not yet on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Perhaps you can assist me. This is the first map that you showed earlier. I think it was indicated -- marked as P16.1 or 161. Maybe that was a mistake in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: It's Exhibit P16.1, and my understanding is it should be on screen now if you press the e-court button.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, we have it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. Thank you. Yes, we can see the map now. You can see where Bratunac is, Pribicevac. You cannot see that it's a mountain or how high it is, but it is a mountain above Srebrenica. So even though it doesn't seem that far on the map, the actual physical distance is about 20 kilometres to Bratunac. The road goes through Sase, as you can see on the map. And from the statements of various witnesses, you can see that a person would need two hours to cover the distance between Bratunac and Pribicevac in either direction. So in those circumstances, it was quite a distance away. You needed two hours to reach Bratunac from Pribicevac and vice versa. Units of the Bratunac Brigade, which were at their positions towards Srebrenica - and I already mentioned this yesterday - did not operate in that direction at all, but operated on a completely different side, towards Nova Kasaba, Sandici, Konjevic Polje, Cerska. These were the directions in which the civilian columns, including probably members of the 28th Division, were pulling out. So there were mixed columns. That is the area around Nova Kasaba and Konjevic Polje that is mentioned in this case as the place where units were intercepted, some military and some military police units intercepted and detained those people, and, as is well-known, were taking them in the direction of Zvornik later. You can see on the map that this is a completely different region. What I believe is very important and needs to be stated is that the operation to search the terrain dealt with by the appeal and the Prosecutor attributed importance to it today as well, especially to the fourth position where the 4th Battalion and the 4th Company were and where the command post was. What is this about? The searching of the terrain under orders of Colonel Blagojevic, and it's an order that we have, was issued to the 1st, 2nd, and the 3rd, was to search the terrain in front of the positions where they were and where they were anticipating combat actions. As far as the fourth, to which my learned friend refers to, Colonel Blagojevic's assignment there was quite different. There wasn't supposed to be any movement of troops or any kind of search of terrain. They were not supposed to leave the place. The order was just to monitor the terrain in the locations they were facing, including Sandici. Blagojevic, when he issued that order, didn't know who would be where and he didn't know who was in Sandici or on the road, that there were already some units on the road, which I think they were police units; he didn't know any of this. So the assignment of this 4th Company, to which he refers to, which was the closest or the furthest away from the command post of the Bratunac Brigade, is quite different. So it was monitoring the terrain, nothing in common with Kravica or Sandici, the units didn't go or enter Kravica or any of these other places. The relative proximity, we're talking about 10 kilometres or several kilometres in relation to the command post, really cannot be any reason for Colonel Blagojevic's responsibility or for the possibility of him knowing or being aware that there was shooting in Kravica and the killing of people who were there. I believe that the Trial Chamber dwelled on this, and in the relevant paragraphs, concluded that there was no evidence of this. And I believe that in that part, for the above-given reasons, the appeal by the Prosecution is without ground. There has been mention here of Blagojevic carrying out blockades of convoys. This was before the Krivaja 95 operation. I believe this has been dealt with in detail in the appeal brief submitted by the Defence, so I will not go into it again. Your Honours will certainly take into account everything contained in the submissions of all sides. I only wish to point out that humanitarian aid convoys were a security issue, that permission was received from the General Staff of the Republika Srpska for the passage of convoys, and only those convoys who had that permission were checked to make sure that this was in compliance with orders. So no one could either prevent or permit something that had not already been dealt with at a higher level. If I understand correctly with reference to the attack on Srebrenica or on the 28th Army, it is quite clear who received issues -- who received orders and instructions from his higher command and passed them on. I only wish to reiterate what has been said in response to a question by His Honour Judge Shahabuddeen as to whether Srebrenica was a UN-protected area at the time. Although the question was put in a different context with relation to sentencing, I wish to point out that there is no contest about this. It really was a UN-protected area, but it was a zone where no military forces were supposed to be present of either side, either the BH federation or the Republika Srpska, yet it is well-known that the 28th Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina was located in that area. We have presented evidence to show that. The circumstance that this was a UN-protected area was used by members of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina to launch attacks from the area or to target certain areas, and there were even cases where civilians were attacked in villages. They would launch the attack from the zone and then withdraw to it again. Therefore, the aim of the Krivaja 95 operation was not the civilian population, but these troops, the 28th Army, which had to be prevented from acting from the UN-protected areas against targets of Republika Srpska. And this was the goal that Blagojevic, as one of the participants and unit commanders, was given. The goals were quite clear. My learned friend often said he was informed -- there is an abundance of evidence to show he was informed. He had to be informed as a commander. These are some of the arguments put forward here. I only wish to say if there is an assumption that he had to be informed, we can see from the communications and the information that reached him what he knew and what he did not know; who was supposed to be informed is another matter. As for evidence that he knew what was going on in Potocari, where he did not set foot either in those days or later on, or what happened later on with the transfer of prisoners, what happened to the buses, it was said that he knew that some buses went outside the area with the women and children and others went in a completely different direction; but we maintain that there is no evidence to show this. Momir Nikolic is a key figure when referring to subordinates who committed crimes. With reference to Momir Nikolic, I wish to draw attention to what I have already stated in my submissions, and that is that as a security officer he acted upon the orders received from his own chain of command in the security organ, and this amounted to 80 per cent of his job. He was acting independently of his commander, to whom he was subordinated indeed, but he was not duty-bound even to inform him of what he was doing when following orders from the security chain of command. And this ran through Beara and the Drina Corps of the security organ, and what Momir Nikolic was doing in those days is something that Blagojevic cannot be held responsible for. That may be the reason why the Court decided that Momir Nikolic was not under the effective control of Vidoje Blagojevic. However, the issue at hand is not whether he was under effective control or not, but that he was actually carrying out tasks which had nothing to do with the Bratunac Brigade. Out of the almost 2.100 members of the brigade, no one participated in any of the activities charged here, apart from Momir Nikolic and the military policemen that he found and gave orders to. And he had the right to do this as a security officer. All the rest, as has been explained in the submissions, the two who were burying bodies were civilians, they were not members of the brigade; they were in the civilian protection. There was a bus driver who was in the civilian protection, not in the brigade. So no member of the brigade participated. As for Momir Nikolic, I refer to paragraph 3.167 in the appeal submissions. It was further stated that he could have found out at least several days later. Blagojevic's task was to prepare his unit for departure to Zepa, and that is what he was focusing on, preparing the unit and departing for Zepa, which is what he did. What he was doing at the time had nothing to do with what happened next in Bratunac, Zvornik, or any other location where mass murders took place. I think I have a few minutes left, Your Honours, and then I will finish. With respect to sentences, in the appeal brief of the 20th of October, the Defence presented its standpoint with respect to what His Honour Judge Meron said yesterday. In paragraph 9.2 it is said that in the final brief that nothing was stated about this in the brief because there was no cooperation with the Defence counsel, and this is and remains a big problem. But everything I said in my response of the 20th of June, 2005, I wish to say that I personally, and as Defence counsel for Vidoje Blagojevic, I feel that those responsible for the tragedy of Srebrenica must be punished, but the true perpetrators must be punished. This Court will certainly establish in proceedings here in The Hague and also in proceedings, to the best of my knowledge, being conducted in Sarajevo, who the perpetrators were. Vidoje Blagojevic, however, was not one of the perpetrators and wishes to prove this in a new and fair trial. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: I thank you. I give -- I see Judge Guney wants to put a question. Please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. [Interpretation] Mr. Domazet, you mentioned the fact that your client, in the appeal, did not have the assistance of a military expert. You also said that had he been able to use the -- a military expert, his powers and the links between him and the acts could have been better defined. Please tell us, do you feel that the lack of such assistance influenced the fair trial; and if so, to what extent and from what aspect. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. Yes, I did state this, and I feel that the testimony of a military expert would have been of extreme importance. It is very important in any case, but particularly in a case such as this one. It could have thrown light on the events in Srebrenica, the positions of the various units, the changes of the initial plan. A military expert for the Defence could certainly have influenced the situation in favour of the defence of the accused, and it is my view, that in addition to the other circumstances and Mr. Blagojevic's personal testimony, which he has not waived, it would have been of exceptional importance to have a military expert in order for the trial to be fair.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If military expert assistance were provided?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if you're referring to Mr. Blagojevic, he did not have an opportunity to address the Court; and whenever he did have such an opportunity, he always stated that the Defence imposed on him was not his own Defence and he asked for his Defence. Mr. Karnavas did not lead this evidence. He did not call such evidence, and it would have been crucial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Thank you. Judge Shahabuddeen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Domazet, you correctly recognised that my references to the status of Srebrenica as being that of a United Nations protected area were made in connection with sentencing, and I take entirely your point that it is the function of the Appeals Chamber to make sure that the real perpetrators of the crime at Srebrenica are punished. But I also bear in mind your remark about the United Nations status of Srebrenica as a protected area to the effect that you did not consider that there was any contest about this. Your words were: "It was really a United Nations protected area." Now, if the Appeals Chamber were to hold that the convictions made by the Trial Chamber of your client were justified, does it follow that the status of Srebrenica as a United Nations protected area has to be taken into account for sentencing purposes?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if I may, I would like to avoid issues of sentencing because of the instructions I have received from my client, who even wanted me not to mention it in my written submissions. As I said, the area truly was a protected area but there was also the 28th Army there and they violated the status of that area because they had their army headquarters within that area and acted from it. The United Nations, unfortunately, did not prevent this, and this was a considerable time before the beginning of this operation. So I feel that this, too, should be taken into account because I still maintain that the civilian population was not the target of the attack. The target was only military, the 28th Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. And that is an order that Blagojevic merely carried out, having received it from a higher command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Thank you. Judge Meron.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Just to clarify your point, counsel, are you telling us that the level of responsibility for an attack, deliberate attack, on the safe zone in Srebrenica was a higher level of command than of Mr. Blagojevic? Belonged to the corps or the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, certainly the attack on Srebrenica and the whole operation was something planned by the General Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska and General Mladic as the Chief of Staff and then the units that were part of the Drina Corps, one of which was the Bratunac Brigade. It is well known that there were other units there, including even police units, and many other units, not just those of the Bratunac Brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Finally, counsel, I must say to you that I'm not persuaded that the absence of military advisor should explain why Mr. Blagojevic, as a colonel of the army and a professional military officer, did not during the trial point to the -- what you claim to be the areas of responsibility of his brigade in contrast to other units. Surely, despite all the difficulties that he had with his counsel, this was an elementary point that he could and should have made clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I really believe that he didn't have the opportunity to do this because, simply - and it can be seen from the transcript - he was not given the floor. And when he did speak and try to explain his status, it was simply said that he cannot talk about that anymore. So for him to put questions or to make suggestions is something that I don't really see as being possible. Based on what happened, he was just a mere observer and didn't have the possibility to do anything. This question is regulated by the rules and the rules were submitted, the rules of service of JNA. So had the Trial Chamber reviewed that, they would have come to the conclusion that an area of responsibility cannot be an area where the Bratunac Brigade was before the combat actions. Once the units were deployed, then each of those units, as part of their assignments, was assigned to a certain area of responsibility. This is something that could have been established without a military expert, but it would have been done properly and more competently had there been a military expert present.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Well, thank you. I will now turn to counsel for Jokic for the response. You have the floor, Mr. Murphy.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Your Honours, Mr. Farrell was good enough to tell me this morning that he did not wish to make any further submissions in regard to the ground of appeal dealing with the Petkovci school, and for that reason I will deal with that extremely briefly. Your Honour, the -- when you look at the Prosecution's ground of appeal alleging that Mr. Jokic should have been convicted with respect to that site also, it -- it fails to plead a ground of appeal of which this Appeals Chamber can really take notice. It simply alleges that the Trial Chamber made an error of fact. Your Honour, I think it's an elementary proposition that the standard of review in the Appeals Chamber is not whether or not the Trial Chamber made an error of fact, in other words -- I'm sorry, I'll allow your colleagues, Mr. President, to confer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. The standard of review is not whether the members of this Chamber might have taken a different view of the facts from the Trial Chamber; the standard is whether the Trial Chamber came to a decision which no reasonable Trial Chamber could have reached. And furthermore, I would suggest in the case of an appeal by the Prosecution, more recent authority -- and I think it's interesting that at one point in their brief they refer to the Tadic appeal, of course as we all know the law has been developed by this Chamber quite a bit since then. And in more recent cases, I think it's become clear that on a Prosecution appeal, they must be able to persuade Your Honours that it was inevitable that the liability of Mr. Jokic on that ground should have been established beyond reasonable doubt. The ground of appeal does not even make that statement. It's not even satisfactory as a matter of pleading within the guide-lines of the practice direction and the other rules that this Chamber requires. It should have been dismissed and should be dismissed without further discussion for that reason. But for the sake of completeness, Your Honour, let me just indicate that the Trial Chamber in fact articulated a very sound reason for reaching the conclusion it did. The Prosecution in its brief contends that there was no real difference between the evidence on the Orahovac site and the Petkovci school site, and that if the -- there was a conviction on one, it should have been followed that there would be a conviction on the other. In fact, however, the Trial Chamber showed -- and I will refer particularly to two paragraphs of the judgement. Firstly, in paragraph 765, the Trial Chamber noted that there was no evidence at all that any members of the Zvornik Brigade were concerned in the killings that took place at Petkovci school and Petkovci dam. And that was further elaborated in a particular finding that the Trial Chamber made at paragraph 345, when they referred to evidence, positive evidence, that members of a completely different unit, namely the 10th Sabotage Department, were actually responsible for those killings. And they noticed also that an officer of the Zvornik Brigade named Milosevic had noted that he did not recognise the soldiers who were guarding the prisoners at that location. So, Your Honour, without more -- without referring to anything else, the Trial Chamber articulated a quite comprehensible reason for distinguishing between those two cases. And given the standard of review, in my submission, Your Honour, that concludes the matter. You can't say that the Trial Chamber was unreasonable to come to that conclusion. They set out, in a quite logical manner, the reasons why they did not find it proved beyond reasonable doubt that Mr. Jokic should be convicted. Your Honour, I submit that given the standard in -- before this Chamber, that should be enough to deny that ground. Let me turn Your Honour now to the matter of appeal, and recognising the difficulty that my learned friend Mr. Domazet had but which I do not have, I would, if I may, respond quite directly to Judge Shahabuddeen's question about the status of Srebrenica as a United Nations protected area. I would like to do so in the context of the issue of sentence as a whole. Firstly, Your Honour, I recognise that there may be exceptional cases in which it would be right for the Appeals Chamber to substitute its own judgement for that of the Trial Chamber on matters of sentence. There may be cases where, quite clearly, the Trial Chamber got it so wrong that intervention is required. But I would respectfully submit that those cases should be few and far between. And for this reason: That the Trial Chamber is entrusted with the primary responsibility for sentencing. They sit through the entire trial. They listen to the evidence. They see the witnesses. And they are in a position to assess the overall criminality of the accused. Your Honours are not in that position. And furthermore, as Your Honours well know, there is no further right of appeal from this Chamber. And if you substitute a sentence, you do so leaving the accused without any further recourse. Now, I do recognise, as I say, that there may be exceptional cases in which that course is justified, but they are truly exceptional and I submit that this case is simply not one of those cases. The Prosecution again has the burden of showing not only that the Trial Chamber passed a sentence with which Your Honours may individually or collectively disagree. They must show that there is something so manifestly wrong with that sentence that the interests of justice demand some intervention by this Chamber. The Prosecution recognises that the Trial Chamber correctly stated the legal test for sentencing, that it depends upon the overall criminality of the accused. Let me note, Your Honour, that the Prosecution -- the Trial Chamber did clearly take into account the whole story of the Srebrenica affair. If you look at the judgement beginning at page 716 -- I'm sorry, paragraph 716, you will see that the Trial Chamber, in relation to Jokic, provides a description of -- beginning with the -- this is in regard to their findings as to Dragan Jokic. They begin to consider his liability, and in paragraph 717 and 718, they describe the -- the detail of what was planned and then they go on over a number of other paragraphs. This is not the only section of the judgement in which the facts are discussed in detail. And in particular response to Judge Shahabuddeen's question about the United Nations protected area, I respectfully point out that the Trial Chamber did, in fact, consider that matter and recorded in the judgement there is a specific paragraph, 100, which I think there was some discussion of yesterday in response to Your Honour's question, where that fact was explicitly referred to. And I would submit, Your Honours, that there is a presumption that the Trial Chamber took into account all the relevant facts that it needed to pronounce its judgement. And when Your Honours have before you a judgement that refers in explicit terms to the entire history of the crimes, and when the Trial Chamber correctly notes that these crimes were committed in the context of a United Nations protected area, and when that Trial Chamber further goes on to say that it has considered the total criminality of the accused in passing its sentence, I submit that Your Honour should make the assumption that when the members of the Trial Chamber considered their judgement, they did so taking into account all of those facts and weighing them in the balance, as they were required to do. The Prosecution has not pointed to any circumstances to rebut the presumption that the Trial Chamber took into account all the facts that it was supposed to; on the contrary, it seems clear from the judgement that they had in mind the circumstances. And so, while I would -- I would submit, Your Honours, that the status of the Srebrenica enclave as a protected area was not so much an aggravating factor as a necessary fact of the context of the crimes, and so it was considered and was properly considered by the Trial Chamber in passing sentence. In the particular case of Mr. Jokic, I would add to that that his involvement in the matter was not concerned with the launching of an attack against the United Nations protected area, regardless of whether or not the 28th Army was there and whether there was any military justification, and I expressly decline to address that manner. I'm not concerned with it. Regardless of the fact of whether that was true or not, that did not affect Mr. Jokic's participation in this case. Your Honours, the Prosecution also points in their brief, although it was not mentioned today, to whether or not it was proper for the Trial Chamber to take into account certain other facts relating to Mr. Jokic's activities helping to demine certain areas after the war, and with particular reference to an incident in which he was said to have safely have conducted a group of Muslim boys through a minefield to ensure their safety. The Prosecution suggests that those are matters that could not be taken into account by the Trial Chamber because they were not mitigating factors relating to the crimes. But Your Honours will bear in mind that the Statute of the Tribunal enjoins that the sentencing court should take into account also the personal characteristics of the accused. And regardless of whether or not these activities had anything to do directly with the events from the 14th to the 17th of July, they gave the Trial Chamber some insight into the kind of man with whom it was dealing. Your Honours have a long accumulated experience at this Tribunal, and you know by now that the accused who come before it are a very diverse collection of people, as are the accused in any court. And it is certainly germane to any responsible sentencing Chamber to consider whether the accused it is dealing with is an evil individual who willingly participated in horrific crimes or, as sometimes happened - and I venture to say as Your Honours know sometimes happens - is basically a good man caught up in bad circumstances and who now finds himself here. And that was a judgement that the Trial Chamber made, and perhaps was entitled to make, and it was their discretion to make. And Your Honours have often observed in the past that comparison with other cases in the field of sentence is generally not very helpful. Certainly to compare Mr. Jokic with Momir Nikolic and Dragan Obrenovic is not, in the facts of this case, a very helpful exercise. The question is not whether Your Honours, if you had been sitting as a Trial Chamber, would have passed the same sentence that this Trial Chamber did. The question is this: Has the Prosecution proved to you that this sentence was so wrong in principle that you have to intervene, regardless of the fact that Mr. Jokic will have no further recourse by way of appeal. And I suggest to you, Your Honours, that the evidence, on the contrary, shows that the Trial Chamber gave a very careful consideration considering all the facts in the light of a long trial and came to a decision, which is plainly defensible and can be sustained on the facts of this case. Your Honour, those are my submissions on the issue of sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Murphy. I give the floor to Judge Meron.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Mr. Murphy, you will recall that earlier I reflected on the level of responsibility as regards to the decision, so regrettable, to attack the safety zone in Srebrenica. You know there are some international criminal tribunals, such as the ICC, International Criminal Court, which contain specific provisions dealing with the criminal character of attack on UN peacekeepers, and therefore Judge Shahabuddeen, I'm very grateful to him for drawing our attention to this problem. I wondered whether you could comment on these points I want to make. As I see paragraph 105 and 106 of the judgement, I read that the intent to attack the safety zone in Srebrenica was one which clearly results -- is attributed to General Mladic and to Mr. Karadzic. Then I read in paragraph 140, this statement: "The Trial Chamber observes the attack on the enclave itself is not the subject matter in this case. The Trial Chamber, therefore, focuses its finding on the involvement of the Bratunac Brigade in relation to the effect of that attack on the civilians." Given these statements in paragraph 140, would you like to clarify your position on this matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Trial Chamber was -- was quite right in the sense that when they considered the activities of the Bratunac Brigade - and Your Honour will see that it was in that particular context - and not, of course, the brigade generally but the -- I suppose in relation to this, the case of Colonel Blagojevic because he was involved in -- with that brigade. But, Your Honour, they were saying in that context that the actual military operation to attack the safe area, the protected area, was not what this case was about. And of course, Your Honour, that -- in the literal sense that was exactly right. My reading of the judgement, though, is the -- that did not cause the Trial Chamber to lose sight of the overall context of the case. When one looks at the other references, the ones Your Honour pointed out as to starting with General Mladic and then the plan filtering down, so to speak, it's quite clear that the Trial Chamber never lost sight of the scale of the crime or the number of the victims or of the status of Srebrenica. But what they did, Your Honour, correctly, was to say, We have to focus on the particular facts before us, recognising that there will be other trials regarding Srebrenica. Your Honours well know that one such trial is underway in this building now, will be resuming I think very shortly. And so like any other episode in this particular war, for example, in the Croatian cases, as Your Honour knows, we have had more than one trial, for example, the trial of General Blaskic and then the trial in which I'm involved Prlic and others going on with different levels of responsibility. So I think all the Trial Chamber was doing here, Your Honour, is to say, Recognising as we do the full nature of the offence we still have to focus primarily on the facts that are presented to us by this particular case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Thank you. Judge Shahabuddeen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Murphy, I want to thank you for your attractive submissions, particularly on sentencing. I do believe we have before us an appeal concerning sentencing, so we must devote some attention to that matter. Now, I'm obliged to Judge Meron for reading out something from the trial judgement to the effect that the attack on the enclave is not the subject matter in this case. Now, appreciating, as I believe you did, the implications of that statement, I would suggest to you that it poses a question which is somewhat contradictory of your first position, that the status of Srebrenica was, in fact, taken into account by the Trial Chamber. If I believe that statement represents the thinking of the Trial Chamber, then it would seem to suggest that the Trial Chamber simply did not consider the status of Srebrenica as having any relevance at all. Secondly, I would ask whether you agree with Mr. Domazet's statement that regarding the status of Srebrenica as a United Nations protected area, the position, as Mr. Domazet said, was that there is no contest about this at all; it was really the United Nations protected area. Do you agree with that statement at all?

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Your Honour, as I understand, I don't want to misquote Mr. Domazet. It may be perhaps that he would like to clarify his statement. As I understood what he said, it was that there was -- clearly there could be no dispute that Srebrenica was a United Nations protected area. On the other hand, I understood him to be suggesting that notwithstanding that, the United Nations had failed to prevent the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina from operating in a military sense from that area and then retreating back into it, which clearly if that were true would have its own implications. Let me make it clear, Your Honour, that regardless of whatever submissions Mr. Domazet makes, I do not make any submissions whatsoever in that regard because I don't believe there's a record that I'm aware of for our purposes which is sufficient to support it one way or the other. Nonetheless -- and I certainly would not for my part, and I think Mr. Jokic would not wish me to in any way minimise the gravity of making an attack on a United Nations protected area, regardless of the circumstances. And that is not part of Mr. Jokic's submissions; I want to make that very clear. What I do submit, Your Honour, is that when one looks at what the Trial Chamber did here, there is no basis for assuming that they did not take that into account when they provided their description of the crimes for which they were passing sentence. Indeed, when one looks at the passage from the Trial Chamber beginning -- judgement beginning at paragraph 100, they make several references to the status of Srebrenica. And in summarising the sentencing, they say that they have taken into account the criminality of the accused. Your Honour, I would submit that one has to presume that the Trial Chamber gave the appropriate gravity, not only to the large number of victims, the circumstances in which the murders were committed, but also the very obvious fact that they were taken from Srebrenica, a United Nations protected area. I think one has to presume that the three professional Judges sitting in the Trial Chamber certainly would be unlikely that they were allowed to forget that fact during the trial and did not forget it. And, Your Honour, unless the Prosecution produces something to say that for some reason they put that out of their minds, I think Your Honours should, with all respect, assume that the Trial Chamber took into account the relevant facts in assessing the criminality of the accused. That was their duty. They said that that was what they were doing, and there was nothing in the judgement to contradict it. And given the limited role of the Appeals Chamber on issues of sentencing, Your Honour, I submit that the -- your approach should be very precise in this area and should be limited to the standard of review that is appropriate for matters of sentence, bearing in mind that this is not a trial de novo, and that it was the responsibility of the Trial Chamber and not this Appellate Chamber to pass the appropriate sentence on the accused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Murphy. If there are no other questions, I will turn to the Prosecution for its reply. You have 20 minutes for your reply, Mr. Farrell.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Most of the submissions that have been heard by the Chamber in response to the Prosecution's submissions are fairly well covered in the brief itself. Many of the submissions in response originate from the briefs as well. I will take a few minutes, but that is all, just to draw to your attention, though I'm sure you're aware of it, of a few matters. Just in relation to my learned friend Mr. Domazet's submissions in relation to the zone of responsibility. I'm sure you're aware that this matter was dealt with in the judgement, and the Court made findings about that, a number of paragraphs. And it's set out in paragraphs 3.66 to 3.67 in the Prosecution's response. In relation to his submissions that there was no searches ongoing by the Bratunac Brigade, once again, I'm sure you're aware by reference to paragraph 742 of the judgement that the 4th Battalion was found by the Trial Chamber to be involved in searching the terrain. In relation to the submissions on the need for an expert, which were in response to His Honour Judge Guney's comments, I just simply note that the Schifanelli report did a address a number of these issues, the objective of Krivaja 95, the role of Momir Nikolic, the status of the Bratunac Brigade, an analysis of its daily reports, the fact of the recent arrival of Mr. Blagojevic as the commander six weeks before the attack, a section on the security and intelligence organs, and a section on the parallel chain of command. Now, I appreciate that Mr. Domazet is arguing that he should have been called as a witness as well, but in my respectful submission, the bottom line is that in light of all the evidence his analysis was simply not accepted. It wasn't that if he had testified it would have made any difference or that there was a need for another expert. Lastly, I can't resist simply commenting on one matter, which is the issue of the safe haven. It appears, if I understand counsel for Mr. Jokic, Mr. Murphy, correctly - and I don't want to put words in his mouth - that he's accepted that it could be an aggravating factor, but that it's taken into account because one has to assume that the Trial Chamber took into account all the evidence as part of context for the purposes of sentencing and that the Court should not interfere with the Trial Chamber's determination unless there is a clear error. As a general proposition, I think Mr. Murphy has stated that correctly, that it could be an aggravating factor. What I -- what is unclear and which I take issue with Mr. Murphy is that -- if it is clearly an aggravating factor and if the Trial Chamber treated it as such, it would have been seen in the judgement as an aggravating factor, in my submission. The Court can take into consideration, I think I'm at issue with Mr. Murphy on this. The Court can take into consideration the context and the background as part of the crime, and if it's necessary to carry out the crime to do other acts, which the accused does, though he's not specifically charged with those other acts, those acts are relevant to the overall conduct of the accused in achieving the crime. And to that extent, it is a relevant factor. I read the Trial Chamber's conclusions at paragraph 140, with respect, as being a statement that the appellants in this case were not charged with the attack on Srebrenica in the sense that it was a violation of the laws or customs of war because of the fact that it may have been -- may have been legitimate to the extent that the attack itself was directed against the 28th Mountain Brigade. But since the Trial Chamber found that since the beginning of the attack and the formulation of Krivaja 95 that it wasn't solely for the attack on the 28th Mountain Brigade, that one of the factors that was included was the elimination of the enclave and the Trial Chamber took into consideration how that carried out, how that came to fruition in determining what was meant by the words "the elimination of the enclave," that the Trial Chamber therefore made a finding that the elimination of the enclave was the objective, that they did it despite the fact that it was protected under the UN, and that if it's found to be an aggravating factor, which in my submission it can be taken into account as part of the actions necessary to achieve their goal in the enclave, then it is a matter which should be taken into account and the only issue I differ with with my learned friend Mr. Murphy is that it appears that it wasn't, though I respect the fact that it wasn't raised by the Prosecution as a specific issue warranting and increasing sentence. I can see that. Those are simply the questions, other than that briefs, I think, deal with the matters adequately. Thank you for your patience.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Farrell.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm sorry to intervene and maybe I was misunderstood on the record. I don't think that I conceded that it was an aggravating circumstance. What I conceded and certainly concede is that it was a relevant consideration for the Trial Chamber to take into account, and it's true, my point is they did take that into account. But I certainly didn't mean to concede, if I did, that it was an aggravating circumstance as that expression is generally understood.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Murphy. Mr. Farrell.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: I stand corrected. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Sorry. I was saying this concludes the submissions by the parties on this appeal. Now, according to the Scheduling Order, both Mr. Blagojevic and Mr. Jokic, if they so wish, can personally address the Court for a maximum of ten minutes each. So I turn to Mr. Blagojevic to ask him if he wants to address personally the Court at this stage.

utterances.speaker: THE APPELLANT BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: So, please, you can present your address, Mr. Blagojevic, for ten minutes, as I said.

utterances.speaker: THE APPELLANT BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Your Honours, I did not have a fair trial before this Tribunal. The fundamental reason for this is that I was not permitted to have a Defence which would fairly and consistently represent my interests before this Tribunal. I dismissed Karnavas on the 7th of April, 2003, by a submission which I delivered to the Registry of the Tribunal on the same day, explaining the reasons for the dismissal. On that date, I interrupted all contact with Karnavas forever. Unfortunately, this submission lay in a drawer for a month or so, and it was only then that the Trial Chamber was informed of it. My problems with Mr. Karnavas began much earlier, as early as March 2002. At the status held on that day, he announced that Suzana Tomanovic would be appointed co-counsel. Up to that point, she had been his interpreter. He did not consult me about this and did not have my agreement to it. In that period and in the ensuing period, problems related to the preparation of my Defence escalated. Karnavas apparently knew about these problems. Yes, I understand. In order to convince me of his allegedly correct work and behaviour, he secured the sudden arrival, in the Detention Unit, of my brother in May 2002. My brother was supposed to persuade me that Karnavas was a good lawyer and that that was how I should take it. However, then and subsequently ensuing events clearly indicated that he is not a good lawyer and that he was not preparing my Defence in my best interest. In spite of my energetic objections, he appointed Suzana Tomanovic as his co-counsel, thus inaugurating his dictatorship. In December 2002, I submitted a written document to the Registry complaining of Karnavas's work, but to no effect. He intensively sabotaged the preparations for my Defence, and I responded to this at each and every Status Conference. Doubts arose, and my lack of trust became more and more pronounced. It seemed that the Judge Schomburg at the Status Conference of the 27th of March, 2003, would take action in order to resolve the problems of my Defence and its work on the case. However, I was surprised by what happened next. Karnavas found a way of excluding Judge Schomburg from the case and everything came to a standstill. Karnavas apparently knew well what he was doing. He procrastinated and delayed the calling of the expert until the beginning of April 2003. When I realised that the experts had done nothing, prepared nothing that would be of use for my Defence, the first day after I realised this, I let them know that they were no longer wanted in my case and I dismissed them. I am linking all this up to my submission of the 7th of April, 2003. At the Status Conference before the trial was about to start, the pre-trial conference, I was in a situation where there was a new judge, Judge Liu, and I had again to make submissions about the hostile actions of Karnavas in the preparation of my defence. On that occasion and at the start of trial I stated clearly before Judge Liu's Trial Chamber that I had no counsel acting on my behalf, and I asked for this to be resolved; however, the resolution of the problem took another two years. As the apex of Karnavas's orgies was the fact that he accused me of fee splitting. As the Appeals Chamber characterised this as the crime of fraud, he published all this in the media, along with my photograph. These accusations were false and malicious, but Karnavas apparently knew that he would profit by them. A year later he himself admitted to having lied. I often asked myself whether anything uglier could have been done than what Karnavas did. In the subsequent period I suffered enormous pressure from representatives of the Registry, who were trying to induce me to agreeing to Karnavas doing whatever he wanted in any way he wanted because they said that's the way it had to be. I was concerned about this, and this caused me serious difficulties. From the day I dismissed Karnavas, I fought for the possibility of choosing a counsel who would act conscientiously in agreement and in compliance of the best standards in acting in my Defence; however, this took two years. The consequences of Karnavas's actions before and during the trial were disastrous for me. My counsel, Mr. Domazet, has spoken about this so I will not repeat what he said. I feel that it is of special importance to note that I was prevented from testifying under oath, and this had negative consequences for me. I should have testified under oath. Your Honours, I do not fear a fair and impartial trial, but my trial was not fair in any segment. In the interests of truth and in the interests of the victims, you should make a fair trial possible for me. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Blagojevic. I give now the floor to Mr. Jokic, if he wants to take the floor, of course.

utterances.speaker: THE APPELLANT JOKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. Thank you. Please allow me to thank you at the beginning for making it possible for me to address you. From the first day when I was summoned by the Prosecution, I responded because I believed then and believe now that I must respond to international justice. It is my duty as a man and officer to cooperate with international justice in order to reach the truth about all the tragic events relating to Srebrenica. In that sense, I would like to believe that this trial has shown how my participation in these unfortunate events -- what it was. During the entire war I fought against negative occurrences, and I emphasise that the robbery of Muslims and also the activities of the Zvornik group who are on trial now in Belgrade. Before that, my life and the life of my family was in danger. I also fought against the incorrect -- improper conduct towards Bosniak detainees. I responded because my profession urged me to do so. I had to be an officer in a town, and I had to be with my people. I did not serve any regime; I was with my people. I tried throughout the war to keep my honour and to preserve my reputation. The entire post-war period I spent on the implementation of the Dayton Peace Accords and practically there is no commission in the work of which I did not take part. Why -- what sort of evidence were you furnished with? I would specifically like to emphasise here my work in the demining commission when I risked my own life. With the successful work of this commission, the return of many Bosniak refugees was made possible. During the post-war work, two persons were killed and nine gravely wounded. I also had my hearing damaged as a consequence of a detonation. During this work of mine, I thought of others first and put myself in the most difficult positions to go from day to day to assignments like this where I could lose my life, and now to sit on this bench is very difficult. I would like to illustrate my work on the reconciliation of our three people with the words of one officer: Now we shake hands, but had we shaken hands in 1992, there would have been no unnecessary victims in Bosnia-Herzegovina. This is something that could be applied to all the politicians in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Your Honours, I was on duty on the 14th of July, 1995, not due to my own will. Had I known what happened would have happened, I would have left my duty no matter what it would have cost me. I myself can say that I did not want anything bad to happen to those people. Your Honours, in that period and throughout the whole war, I saved weak Bosniaks. I did not support killings then. I said that I had saved a group of boys whom I fed, took them through firing positions safely, and handed over to the forces of the Bosnia-Herzegovina army. You have had evidence of all of this in the course of the trial. I would like to emphasise that during my detention in The Hague I have lost practically my whole family. My mother and my sister died, and I was unable to be with them during their last hours. My son is now living in Zvornik alone. I am sorry for all the victims, and I am aware that the tragedy of Srebrenica will always accompany the history of the Serbian people. I understand that the Appeals Chamber cannot re-try anew this case, but I stand by my innocence and I stand by that now. I know that there was some witnesses who appeared who lied about me and whose testimony was prejudicial to me. Pero Petrovic did not speak the truth, and I would like you to accept my evidence. He was a witness who had been coerced or blackmailed. Dragan Obrenovic testified falsely. He did not meet me at the command on the 15th of July, as he said, but on the 15th in the morning he was at the brigade command - and this is in the duty log-book - and he issued all the orders. I was the officer on duty at the time. Your Honours, I would especially like to say that in the trial we proved that I was the only person at the command when there is an extraordinary situation. Everybody is there. The functions of the duty officers have nothing to do with commanding the units. I never issued any orders to anyone, although I have considerable respect for the Trial Chamber, I did not commit the crimes that I was charged with and I have nothing to reproach myself with in relation to Srebrenica throughout the whole war, and then I was saving Bosniaks and not killing them. I am not an evil person and I do not hate anyone. At today's hearing and yesterday's hearing, the Prosecution is again trying to put me in the function of a person who was some sort of command or directed something. If anybody was in that position, then it was Dragan Obrenovic. Regardless of what your verdict is, I am still going to struggle for the reconciliation of Croats, Serbs, and Bosniaks and for truth about Srebrenica. Thank you for listening to me, and I would like to wish the best of health and fortune to everyone in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Jokic. We come now to the end of this appeals hearing. Before closing, I would like to thank the parties for their helpful contribution to assisting the Appeals Chamber in considering this appeal; the court officers and staff for their cooperation throughout the hearing; and last but not least, our interpreters for their invaluable assistance in making dialogue between the parties and the Bench possible. The Appeals Chamber will render its judgement in due course. The hearing on this appeal stands adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: adjourned at 11.53 a.m.
